name: Saudi Arabia
governanceModel: State-directed AI strategy; government messaging in 2026 emphasizes execution over planning
debateTopics: Shift from AI strategy to execution — can HUMAIN build in one year what took 20?
Chip access as part of Gulf compute diplomacy
Sovereign Arabic models versus dependence on foreign hardware and hyperscalers
overview:
Saudi Arabia's Cabinet designated 2026 the 'Year of Artificial Intelligence,' which government statements describe as marking a shift from strategy to execution of the National Strategy for Data and AI (NSDAI), led by SDAIA (the Saudi Data and AI Authority) since 2019 across six pillars: ambition, competencies, policies, investment, innovation and ecosystem. SDAIA's board is chaired by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, and there is no binding AI-specific statute; the closest binding instrument is the SDAIA-supervised Personal Data Protection Law, enforceable since September 2024.

HUMAIN — launched in May 2025 as the Public Investment Fund's principal sovereign AI vehicle and framed in some coverage as a roughly $100B undertaking — consolidated some of Aramco Digital's AI assets at founding; Saudi Aramco separately agreed in a later, distinct transaction reported in late 2025 to acquire a significant minority stake, with PIF retaining majority ownership. Through 2025–2026 HUMAIN assembled an unusually broad compute-supplier stack — NVIDIA (reported at up to several hundred thousand GPUs over five years, with 18,000 GB300 chips delivered first), AMD (a roughly $10B, 500MW commitment), AWS (a $5B-plus 'AI Zone'), and Qualcomm (200MW of AI200/AI250 inference from 2026) — and was approved alongside the UAE's G42 in November 2025 to buy up to 35,000 NVIDIA Blackwell chips. On the model side, SDAIA's National Center for AI developed the ALLaM family of Arabic-first LLMs (distributed via Microsoft Azure and IBM watsonx), with HUMAIN increasingly positioned as their commercial production and distribution channel. Recent infrastructure milestones include the KAUST-hosted Shaheen III supercomputer and the roughly $2.7B, 480MW Hexagon data centre in Riyadh, which broke ground in January 2026 and is described in Saudi state and trade press as among the world's largest government data facilities by capacity.

currentDirection.summary: Saudi Arabia does not appear to be introducing new binding AI rules; instead, government statements have emphasized rapid execution of its existing strategy, with HUMAIN CEO Tareq Amin stating a goal of building in one year what previously took two decades.

recentDevelopments.text: The GCC (Gulf Cooperation Council) steering committee is reported to have announced a common regional AI policy — shared principles on AI ethics, data privacy, security and cross-border cooperation among member states — as a step toward a unified Gulf AI strategy. Saudi Arabia, whose own approach already anticipates GCC-wide alignment, would be a central participant, though details on scope, timeline and enforcement remain thin in early reporting.

Cabinet designates 2026 the 'Year of Artificial Intelligence', marking a shift from strategy to execution of the National Strategy for Data and AI; SDAIA issues national guidelines to unify the year's initiatives across government.

HUMAIN's compute-supplier stack scales toward activation through 2026: alongside NVIDIA (reported at up to several hundred thousand GPUs over five years) and an AMD commitment of roughly $10B for 500MW of capacity, HUMAIN plans to deploy 200MW of Qualcomm AI200/AI250 inference solutions from 2026, and AWS's $5B-plus 'AI Zone' infrastructure is set to come online — a landmark concentration of advanced compute in one sovereign vehicle.

The roughly $2.7B, 480MW Hexagon data centre breaks ground in Riyadh — described in Saudi state and trade press as among the world's largest government data facilities by capacity — while the KAUST-hosted Shaheen III supercomputer (ranked 18th on the November 2025 Top500) anchors national research compute.
HUMAIN and G42 jointly approved to purchase up to 35,000 NVIDIA Blackwell (GB300) chips.

SDAIA's National Center for AI extends the ALLaM family of Arabic-first LLMs — recognised as a leading Arabic-language model on the Arabic MMLU benchmark and distributed via Microsoft Azure AI Foundry and IBM watsonx — with HUMAIN increasingly positioned as its commercial production and distribution channel.
SDAIA reports growing government adoption of AI services under the Year of AI, part of the National Strategy for Data and AI's execution phase.
DISAI 2026 programme (Qualcomm, Aramco, RDIA and HUMAIN) supports deep-tech AI and IoT startups, drawing more than 124 applicants.

policyAndRegulation.title: 2026 'Year of Artificial Intelligence'

policyAndRegulation.title: Personal Data Protection Law (PDPL)
policyAndRegulation.summary: Saudi Arabia's binding legal framework most relevant to AI-related data governance; enacted by Royal Decree M/19 (2021), amended by Royal Decree M/148 (2023), and fully enforceable since 14 September 2024. Supervised by SDAIA, which issued 48 enforcement decisions in its first year.

researchEcosystem.summary: Saudi AI infrastructure investment — including the Shaheen III supercomputer and the Hexagon data centre — appears to have outpaced distinct academic AI research institute-building. KAUST (King Abdullah University of Science and Technology) remains the country's leading research university and hosts Shaheen III, though the scope of any dedicated AI research programme there has not been independently verified beyond this.

debates.topic: Shift from AI strategy to execution — can HUMAIN build in one year what took 20?
debates.summary: HUMAIN's leadership has publicly set a goal of building in a single year what previously took two decades — a timeline that industry observers have generally characterized as extremely aggressive.
debates.expanded: Consolidating some of Aramco's AI assets under HUMAIN, alongside large compute purchases and one of the region's largest data-centre construction projects, reflects a bet that state-directed speed can compress typical AI infrastructure build-out timelines. Whether execution matches the ambition — rather than just headline infrastructure statistics — remains an open question, and independent assessment of progress against the stated one-year goal is not yet available.

debates.topic: Chip access as part of Gulf compute diplomacy
debates.summary: Saudi Arabia's access to advanced AI chips, like the UAE's, appears to depend on case-by-case US diplomatic approval rather than settled, general trade policy.
debates.expanded: The November 2025 approval for HUMAIN (alongside G42) to purchase advanced NVIDIA chips followed direct diplomatic engagement, including a Saudi Crown Prince visit. This suggests Saudi Arabia's compute access may be a function of bilateral relations as much as commercial terms — a dependency that could shift with US political change.

debates.topic: Sovereign Arabic models versus dependence on foreign hardware and hyperscalers
debates.summary: Saudi Arabia pairs a genuine sovereign-model effort — SDAIA's ALLaM Arabic LLMs — with near-total reliance on imported chips and foreign cloud platforms for both training compute and distribution, a tension common across the Gulf's AI strategies.
debates.expanded: ALLaM gives the Kingdom a credible Arabic-first model recognised on benchmarks such as Arabic MMLU, and HUMAIN is being positioned as its commercial channel. Yet the underlying compute depends on US-approved NVIDIA and AMD hardware and AWS/Qualcomm partnerships, and the models are largely distributed through Microsoft Azure and IBM watsonx. Whether this produces durable sovereign capability — as opposed to Saudi-branded services running on foreign silicon and clouds — remains an open question, and is sharpened by the fact that advanced-chip access still turns partly on case-by-case US approval.
